name: GitHub
summary: Registering a GitHub OAuth app is a form on your account settings and takes minutes. The docs list no review step. The real decision is whether to use an OAuth app or a GitHub App, which GitHub's docs recommend considering first.
difficultyWhy: Self-serve form, no documented review. The only complexity is choosing between an OAuth app and a GitHub App, and organization access policies.

approval.details: The registration page does not mention any review or approval process. Organizations may still restrict third-party OAuth apps (see blockers; unconfirmed).

requirements.text: A GitHub account (personal or organization) that owns the app. One user or org can own up to 100 OAuth apps.
Application name, Homepage URL and Authorization callback URL. Up to 10 callback URLs are allowed.
Decide on 'Expire user access tokens' (on by default) and optional Device Flow.
OAuth apps can only act on behalf of a user; GitHub Apps can also act independently and use fine-grained permissions and short-lived tokens. GitHub recommends considering a GitHub App first.
A client secret is generated after registration and must be stored server-side.

steps.title: Decide: OAuth app or GitHub App
steps.detail: If you need fine-grained repo access or actions without a signed-in user, create a GitHub App instead. For simple 'act as the user' access, an OAuth app is fine.

steps.title: Open Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps > New OAuth App
steps.detail: Click your profile picture, then Settings, then Developer settings in the sidebar.

steps.title: Fill in name, homepage URL, callback URL
steps.detail: Use only information you consider public. The callback URL must be your integration's redirect endpoint.

steps.title: Choose token expiry and Device Flow, then Register application
steps.detail: Leave token expiry enabled unless your integration cannot handle refresh tokens yet.

steps.title: Store the client ID and secret in your secrets manager
steps.detail: Never commit them. Configure them in the integration that will run the OAuth flow.

blockers.issue: Users in an organization cannot authorize your app
blockers.fix: Organizations can restrict third-party OAuth apps; an org owner must approve the app. (Unconfirmed in docs checked here; verify in the org's third-party access settings.)
The redirect URI sent in the authorize request must match a registered callback URL. Register every environment (local, staging, prod), up to 10.

agentCan: Draft the registration values (name, homepage, callback URLs) and the scope list.
Wire the client ID/secret into your integration config and test the flow once credentials exist.
developerMust: Be signed in to GitHub (2FA applies) and submit the registration form.
Own the decision between OAuth app and GitHub App.
uncertain: Client secret handling is not stated on the fetched page.
Org third-party restriction behaviour was not verified against a real org.
